name: KOR-Bench
ability_definition: The ability to apply general rules to specific problems to produce answers that make sense.

task_realism.reasoning: The core act matches the definition: read a newly stated general rule and apply it to a specific instance. But the task content is synthetic. It covers invented math operators, novel logic systems, cipher procedures, Sudoku-style puzzles and fictional-world counterfactuals. Workplace deduction looks different. Examples include applying tax codes, building codes, clinical guidelines, contract clauses, compliance policies or troubleshooting procedures to real cases. Those rules are domain-embedded and interact with background knowledge, which KOR-Bench deliberately strips out.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: The rules are handed over complete, unambiguous and self-contained in the prompt. The task is single-turn with no tools, no retrieval and no need to find which rule applies. There are no stakes and no interaction with colleagues or documents. Real work usually requires locating the relevant rule among many and resolving conflicting or vague provisions. It also means dealing with incomplete case facts. The one real-work feature KOR-Bench shares is that the rules are unfamiliar and cannot be pattern-matched from memory. This mirrors applying a new policy or regulation.

construct_coverage.reasoning: The benchmark isolates rule-to-instance application well. It spans five diverse rule types, and its knowledge-orthogonal design reduces contamination by memorized answers. This is a genuine strength for measuring the ability itself. However, cipher and operation tasks lean procedural (algorithm execution) rather than inferential. The benchmark also omits the 'answers that make sense' side of the definition: sanity-checking conclusions against context, handling exceptions, interpreting rule intent, and reasoning when rules are underspecified. The result is a solid but partial slice of the ability.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are compact puzzle-style rule statements with toy problems. Outputs are exact short answers, such as a decrypted string, a number or a grid fill, extracted for automatic matching. Workplace artifacts are different. They are case files, regulations, specifications and tickets. The expected outputs are written determinations, justifications, decisions or reports that explain how the rule applies.

transferability_reasoning: KOR-Bench cleanly isolates applying novel explicit rules to specific problems, largely free of memorized knowledge, so it captures the essence of deductive reasoning better than most benchmarks. Its tasks, however, are synthetic puzzles, ciphers and invented operators with fully specified rules and exact-match answers. It therefore misses the messy rule retrieval, ambiguity resolution and sense-checking that dominate workplace deduction. Strong KOR-Bench performance signals the underlying capacity but transfers only modestly to real-world rule application.

2025.human_reference: Relevant educated workforce: college-educated knowledge workers who routinely apply explicit rules or procedures to specific cases (analysts, compliance and QA staff, technical workers), working carefully under a single-attempt condition.
